title: Two poems about the rainy season
text:
Poem A: The First Rain

For six long months the sky held its breath.
The paddy fields cracked like old plates,
the river shrank to a thin brown thread,
and dust lay down on everything
as if it planned to stay.

Then, one afternoon in November,
the air turned heavy and sweet.
A cloud the colour of wet slate
rolled over the volcano,
and the first fat drops hit the ground
like coins tossed onto a table.

Tik. Tak. Tik-tik-tak.

The thirsty earth gulped them down
and breathed out a smell
older than any of us:
warm, green, wonderful.

Grandmother stood in the doorway
and laughed, and laughed,
holding out her hands
as if the rain were an old friend
come home at last.

My little brother ran outside
with his face turned up and his mouth wide open,
and the frogs, who had hidden under stones
all through the dry months,
began their loud, croaking applause.

Tonight the gutters are singing.
The fields are drinking deeply.
Tomorrow, Father says, we plant.

Poem B: By February

It rained on Monday morning,
it rained on Tuesday too;
by Wednesday every sock I owned
was soggy, through and through.

The street became a chocolate stream,
the stream became a lake;
the frogs held concerts every night
and kept the town awake.

My schoolbooks smell of mushrooms now,
my towel will not dry;
the clouds have parked above our house
and will not leave the sky.

Our cat sits sulking by the door,
the hens refuse to play;
the only ones still smiling are
the ducks across the way.

I asked the rain to take a rest
and try another town;
it only laughed and stamped its feet
and poured more water down.

In August, when the fields were dust,
I begged the clouds for rain;
now I would give my favourite toy
to see the sun again.
